question: Compare the average and median price_usd in the product prices dataset, then explain why they differ.
answer: The average (mean) price_usd in the product prices dataset is 105.041 [D1], while the median price_usd is 58.955 [D2]. The mean is influenced by extreme values, whereas the median is not. [S2] In a right-skewed distribution like this dataset, with a few very high prices, the mean is typically larger than the median. [S2] This difference indicates the presence of outliers or extreme values in the dataset, which pull the mean upwards [S2] [S1].

citations.title: Statistics Robust Summaries
citations.text:
The mean is the sum of the values divided by their count, so every value, including extreme ones,
pulls it. The median is the middle value of the sorted data and ignores how far the extremes lie.
When a distribution is right-skewed (a long tail of a few very large values, as with prices or
incomes) a few large values drag the mean upward while the median stays near the typical value, so
the mean exceeds the median. When the data are symmetric the two are close. A large gap between the
mean and the median is therefore a quick diagnostic for skew or outliers. For skewed data, report
the median (or both) because it better describes a typical observation.

S3.title: Statistics Lecture Notes
S3.text: 1. Descriptive Statistics Descriptive statistics summarize a dataset. Measures of central tendency are the mean (the sum of the values divided by the number of values), the median (the middle value of the sorted data) and the mode (the most frequent value). The mean is sensitive to outliers; the median is robust to them. For right-skewed data such as incomes the mean is usually larger than the median. Measures of spread describe variability. The range is maximum minus minimum. The variance averages squared deviations from the mean, and the standard deviation is the square root of the variance, so it has the same units as the data. The interquartile range (IQR) is Q3 minus Q1 and is used to flag outliers: a common rule marks values below Q1 - 1.5 * IQR or above Q3 + 1.5 * IQR.
